claims.text: In situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction can be used to study high-temperature oxidation behavior and phase stability.
HTXRD provides real-time monitoring of phase transformations and oxide formation during heating.
The material initially is an as-synthesized, primary single-phase high-entropy alloy.
The initial phase may be BCC or B2 as determined at room temperature.
The material can be heated to approximately 850–1100 °C in air or vacuum while XRD data are collected.
A heating rate of about 15 °C/min with periodic stabilization for diffraction acquisition can be used.
Heating can produce new oxide phases such as MnO, Cr2O3, or spinels.
Lattice-parameter shifts and the appearance or disappearance of diffraction peaks provide signals of phase transformations.
Increasing temperature increases atomic mobility and diffusion rates.
Increased atomic mobility and diffusion lead to oxidation and phase transitions.
HTXRD detects oxidation and phase transformation through changes in peak position and intensity and through the emergence of new reflections.
Oxide peaks and peak-position shifts will appear at specific high-temperature thresholds.
Changes in diffraction patterns can indicate oxidation kinetics.
The room-temperature baseline pattern has well-defined lattice parameters and no oxide-related peaks.
Air and vacuum environments can shift the onset temperature and sequence of oxidation or phase changes.
Changing the heating rate may shift the onset temperature of oxidation or phase change.
Exact transformation temperatures may depend on alloy composition and experimental setup.
Minor phases or low-volume-fraction oxides may be undetectable when they fall below the instrument's sensitivity.
Diffraction patterns can be collected every 50 °C up to 1100 °C under both air and vacuum.
The absence of detectable diffraction changes throughout the tested range in both environments would falsify the effectiveness of HTXRD for monitoring oxidation behavior and phase stability.

contradictions.description: The uncertainty field acknowledges that transformations or low-volume-fraction oxides may fall below instrumental sensitivity, whereas the falsification rule treats the absence of detected changes as decisive evidence that HTXRD is ineffective. A null result could instead reflect true material stability or insufficient detection sensitivity.
